topic: Why you hear your name across a loud party
hook: You're at a loud party, ignoring every voice in the room.
visual_style: Stylized 3D animated film look, Pixar-quality expressive cartoon characters, bold saturated colors, warm colorful lighting, clean simple backgrounds

blocks.narration: You're at a loud party, ignoring every voice in the room. Then someone across the room says your name, and you hear it instantly.
blocks.visual: A bored young man at a loud house party

shots.visual: A cartoon young man with big expressive eyes and messy brown hair stands in a crowded, noisy house party holding a red cup, looking bored and tuned out
shots.action: He rolls his eyes and sighs while partygoers chatter around him

shots.visual: Across a crowded colorful party, a cheerful cartoon young woman with curly red hair cups her hands around her mouth to call out to someone
shots.action: She calls out loudly; a glowing golden ripple of sound bursts from her hands and travels across the room through the crowd; camera whips to follow it

shots.visual: Extreme close-up of the same young man's face at the party, eyes snapping wide open in surprise
shots.action: His eyes snap wide and his eyebrows shoot up as he spins toward the sound; fast crash zoom into his face

blocks.narration: Scientists call it the cocktail party effect. In nineteen fifty-nine, a third of people heard their name in a voice they were ignoring.
blocks.visual: A cartoon brain in a spotlight

shots.visual: A cute cartoon human brain character with big eyes and a tiny party hat stands on a stage under a spotlight, colorful sound waves swirling around it
shots.action: The brain character bobs to the music and the colorful sound waves swirl around it in rings

shots.visual: A 1950s psychology lab in warm retro colors: a cartoon volunteer wearing big vintage headphones sits at a table while a researcher in a lab coat watches beside a spinning reel-to-reel tape recorder
shots.action: The reels spin, the volunteer concentrates hard, the researcher leans in and scribbles on a clipboard

shots.visual: Close-up of the same 1950s volunteer with brown hair and an orange shirt, wearing the big vintage headphones, one ear cup glowing golden, warm retro lab blurred behind
shots.action: A golden glow pulses from one ear cup and the volunteer's eyes dart toward it, eyebrows rising in recognition

blocks.narration: Your brain filters every sound, but it never stops scanning for the words that matter to you. Follow for one brain fact a day.
blocks.visual: Inside the brain, a control room

shots.visual: Inside a cartoon brain, a cozy control room: a tiny friendly robot operator sits at a big mixing desk full of glowing colored sliders
shots.action: The robot pulls most sliders down so the glowing sound bars drop, then taps the one slider that stays up, glowing gold

shots.visual: The same young man at the party, now turned toward the camera with a big knowing smile, warm party lights behind him
shots.action: He grins, raises his red cup toward the camera and nods as if he gets it

shots.visual: The same cute cartoon brain character with a tiny party hat, standing in a spotlight facing the camera
shots.action: The brain waves at the camera with both hands, winks and does a little hop

cta: Follow for one brain fact a day.

captions.hook_line: Ever heard your name across a loud room? That's your brain's filter at work 🧠
captions.body: Psychologists call it the cocktail party effect. In Neville Moray's 1959 experiment, about a third of people noticed their own name in a message they were told to ignore.
captions.share_line: Send this to the friend who always hears their name.

youtube_title: Why You Hear Your Name at a Party

sources.claim: Moray (1959), own name in the unattended message
